input.objective: Calculate BCE for each label and show the selected branch

chunks.label: Authored development source
chunks.text: For a binary label y and class-1 probability p in (0,1), BCE is −[y ln p + (1−y)ln(1−p)]. When y=1 only −ln p remains; when y=0 only −ln(1−p) remains.

annotation.rationale: Procedural: the objective asks you to calculate BCE for each label, an operation to carry out. Conceptual: showing the selected branch needs the reason the label removes one term.

support.quote: Calculate BCE for each label
When y=1 only −ln p remains

input.objective: Explain the equivalence of likelihood fitting and minimising NLL

chunks.label: Authored development source
chunks.text: Taking the log turns a product into a sum. Log is strictly increasing for positive inputs, so the maximisers are unchanged. Negating reverses maximisation to minimisation.

annotation.rationale: Conceptual: the equivalence rests on reasons (log is strictly increasing; negation reverses maximisation). Procedural: taking the log and negating are algebraic steps that can be practised.

support.quote: Log is strictly increasing for positive inputs, so the maximisers are unchanged.

input.objective: Explain the analogy's correspondence and limits

chunks.label: Authored analogy
chunks.text: Think of BCE as a penalty for confidently backing the wrong label. This captures the direction of the penalty, but BCE specifies a logarithmic magnitude rather than an arbitrary penalty.

annotation.rationale: Analogous: the source states an explicit comparison (BCE as a penalty for confidently backing the wrong label). Conceptual: explaining where it fails needs the logarithmic definition.

support.quote: Think of BCE as a penalty for confidently backing the wrong label.

chunks.label: Authored development source
chunks.text: BCE penalises assigning low probability to the true label.

annotation.rationale: Conceptual: the objective asks you to explain a principle about what the loss penalises. No comparison is supplied, so creating your own analogy is optional and would be yours, not the source's.

support.quote: BCE penalises assigning low probability to the true label.

input.objective: Explain how this example supports the claim that equal accuracy can conceal different loss

chunks.label: Authored illustration
chunks.text: For y=1, probabilities 0.8 and 0.6 both predict class 1 under a 0.5 threshold, but their losses are approximately 0.22314 and 0.51083.

annotation.rationale: Supporting evidence: the computed example illustrates the claim that equal accuracy can conceal different loss. Conceptual: the claim itself is about what BCE measures. The example is an illustration, not a calibration result.

support.quote: both predict class 1 under a 0.5 threshold
equal accuracy can conceal different loss
